title: Urgent stability patch policy and branching guidelines
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background:
This ticket codifies an operational policy and concrete branching/patching conventions for urgent stability fixes (hotfixes) and rollbacks across our release and LTS channels. We need a single source of truth that ties severity, ownership, branch naming, CI gating, canary rollout steps, backport rules, and post-release obligations together so engineers can move quickly and safely under pressure.

Goals:
- Define severity tiers with measurable triggers and target time-to-patch windows.
- Standardize branch naming and backport matrix for both stable releases and LTS channels.
- Prescribe a staged rollout/canary sequence with automatic rollback thresholds plus a manual rollback playbook.
- Ensure CI, tests, and release notes requirements are explicit to avoid regressions during hotfix flow.
- Clarify communication responsibilities and postmortem timelines.

Severity tiers and response objectives (recommended):
- Sev-Critical (S0): Customer-facing data corruption, production data loss, regulatory breach, or widespread outage (>= 50% of requests failing). Response owner: on-call SRE + on-call runtime lead. Target: mitigated within 1 hour; patch PR within 4 hours; production rollout within 6 hours.
- Sev-High (S1): Major functionality degraded (high error rates or severe latency affecting a large subset). Owner: on-call runtime lead. Target: mitigated within 2 hours; patch PR within 24 hours; rollout within 48 hours.
- Sev-Medium (S2): Non-critical but material regressions (subset of customers impacted, or increased cost without correctness loss). Owner: feature owner. Target: patch within 3-7 days.
- Sev-Low (S3): Cosmetic/non-blocking issues. Address in the next minor/patch release cadence.

Triage checklist (first 30 minutes):
1) Confirm incident severity and customer impact using dashboards and error traces.
2) Assign response owner and notify PagerDuty and #release-ops channel.
3) If reproducible, produce minimal repro steps or synthetic test.
4) Decide immediate mitigation (feature flag, traffic routing, throttle) before code patch if possible.

Branching & naming conventions:
- Hotfix branches must be cut from the active release or LTS branch that is affected (never from main). Use: hotfix/<release>-ENG-<ticket>-short-desc (e.g., hotfix/1.20.2-ENG-40712-kv-cache-fix).
- LTS backports: create backport branches off the LTS branch (lts/<major>.<minor>) with the same PR pattern and reference the originating hotfix ticket.
- Patch semantic versioning: hotfixes should bump patch version (x.y.Z -> x.y.Z+1). If hotfix includes behavior changes with compatibility risk, evaluate minor bump and coordinate with PM.

CI & testing requirements before merge:
- Run full unit and integration test suites including KV cache regression tests and model-serving smoke tests.
- Add a targeted e2e test demonstrating the original failure scenario (must pass locally and in CI).
- For runtime/CUDA/kernel changes, require a stage-specific GPU test matrix (NVIDIA A100 + fallback quantized runner where applicable).
- PR must include: description of the regression, link to incident timeline, a changelog line, and a test plan for rollout.

Backport policy and matrix (decision rules):
- Always backport to the oldest supported LTS branch that could be affected and to the actively released branch that contains affected code.
- If the hotfix touches non-LTS code paths or experimental features, evaluate impact before backport. Backport only when risk of regression is acceptable.
- Backport ordering: primary release branch -> LTS newest -> older LTS (stop when the code paths diverge significantly).

Staged rollout (recommended automated flow):
1) Internal smoke: deploy to internal testing cluster and run smoke scripts (10-30 min).
2) Canary 1: 1% of production traffic for 15-30 minutes, monitor error rate, latency, and key traces.
3) Canary 2: 10% traffic for 30-60 minutes, run full SLO checks and sampling of outputs.
4) Broad rollout: 50% for 30 minutes, then 100% if SLOs hold.

Automatic rollback triggers (examples):
- Error rate increase > 5x baseline AND absolute error rate > 1% sustained for 5 minutes.
- P95 latency regression > 3x baseline AND absolute P95 > configured SLO for 10 minutes.
- New exception classes indicative of crash/oom/data corruption.
- Any customer-reported data loss or regulatory exposure.

Manual rollback playbook (when automatic rollback is insufficient):
1) Identify earliest safe previous tag that passed all canaries.
2) Coordinate with on-call infra to scale down the bad revision (route traffic to the previous revision) and lock autoscaling/policy changes.
3) If data model changes occurred, assess irreversible migrations; consider compensating actions instead of binary rollback.
4) Communicate to stakeholders: update incident channel, post to status.redwood.ai if external impact, and notify affected customers via customer-success.

Communications & post-release obligations:
- During incident: use #release-ops and the PagerDuty incident. Post short updates every 30 minutes for Sev-Critical and hourly for Sev-High until stable.
- After patch release: create a PR summary in the ticket, update the public changelog (if customer-facing), and add an internal changelog entry referencing LTS backports.
- Postmortem: for Sev-Critical and Sev-High incidents, publish a blameless postmortem within 7 days and an action-plan with owners within 14 days.

Operational checklist for the release engineer merging a hotfix:
- Verify branch originates from correct release/LTS branch.
- Confirm CI green for release-specific GPU matrix.
- Ensure at least one code owner review and a runtime lead approval.
- Attach runbook steps and monitoring dashboard to the PR description.
- Tag the PR with release notes and update semantic version bump file.

Edge cases and guidance:
- If a hotfix is urgent but the fix touches multi-component contracts (console + runtime + routing), coordinate a cross-team emergency MR that includes a compatibility test harness.
- If backport introduces a third-party dependency bump, run a compatibility sweep and delay backport until compatibility confirmed, unless severity mandates immediate backport.

Metrics & telemetry to monitor during rollouts:
- Error-rate by route and model.
- Latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) and spike detection.
- Token-per-second throughput and queue/backpressure metrics.
- Request-level trace sampling for the fixed code path.

Follow-ups (action items):
- Create CI job templates for hotfix GPU matrix (owner: infra team, ENG-40745).
- Add hotfix branch linter to pre-merge checks (owner: platform infra, ENG-40746).
- Publish a condensed hotfix one-pager for on-call and embed in the PagerDuty runbook (owner: SRE, ENG-40747).

Rationale and trade-offs:
- We prefer cutting hotfix branches from the release branch to avoid accidental inclusion of unshipped changes on main. This increases backport work but reduces risk of introducing unrelated changes.
- Automated staged rollouts reduce Blast Radius; however, short canaries may miss rare failures — combine with trace sampling and long-running synthetic checks.

Acceptance criteria for this ticket:
- A documented policy page published in Confluence with the severity matrix, branch naming, CI gating checklist, rollout steps, rollback thresholds, and postmortem timeline.
- A sample hotfix PR template added to the runtime repo and a pipeline that executes the recommended GPU test matrix.
- Team review and approval from Release Engineering, SRE, and Runtime leads.

Links and references included in attachments.
